full_text_en:
Yang Yanhui v. China Southern Airlines Co., Ltd. and Shanghai Minhui Aviation Service Co., Ltd. — Dispute over Passenger Transport Contract

Plaintiff: Yang Yanhui, female, 27 years old, staff member of Shanghai Huiye Law Firm, residing at Shaanxi North Road, Shanghai.

Defendant: China Southern Airlines Co., Ltd. Domicile: Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport.
Legal Representative: Yan Zhiqing, Chairman of the Company.

Defendant: Shanghai Minhui Aviation Service Co., Ltd. Domicile: No. 2088 Huashan Road, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Cheng Jishu, Chairman of the Company.

Plaintiff Yang Yanhui filed a lawsuit with the Xuhui District People's Court of Shanghai against Defendants China Southern Airlines Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as China Southern Airlines) and Shanghai Minhui Aviation Service Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Minhui Company) due to a dispute over a passenger transport contract.

Plaintiff's Allegations: Before the Spring Festival, intending to gather with alumni, I booked a ticket to Xiamen by phone through Defendant Minhui Company, and explicitly stated that I would board at Shanghai Hongqiao Airport. When a staff member of Minhui Company delivered the ticket the next day, they did not specifically indicate that the boarding location was not Hongqiao. The departure place stated on the ticket was "Shanghai PVG". When I arrived at Hongqiao Airport on time, I discovered that the flight was to be taken at Pudong Airport. I immediately requested a transfer at the China Southern Airlines office at Hongqiao Airport. The office staff said that this was a ticket purchased at a 10% discount and could not be transferred, but could be refunded and then changed to another flight. Having no choice, I applied for a refund and simultaneously purchased a full-price ticket for another flight that day. I was stranded at the airport for six hours before arriving in Xiamen. After returning to Shanghai, I went to China Southern Airlines to process the refund and was told that according to regulations, only 80% of the ticket price could be refunded. I believe that the refund and my forced six-hour stay at the airport were entirely caused by the Defendants' failure to clearly inform me of the boarding location. The actions of the two Defendants seriously infringed upon my lawful rights and interests. I request the court to order the two Defendants to refund the full ticket price of RMB 770, compensate me for economic losses of RMB 700, and order the two Defendants to indicate the airport name on the tickets they sell.

Defendant China Southern Airlines' Defense: According to the regulations of the Civil Aviation Administration of China (CAAC), China Southern Airlines' tickets are all issued using automatic ticketing machines. The automatic ticketing machine cannot print Chinese airport names on tickets, so the airport code PVG is used. As the carrier, China Southern Airlines has fulfilled its obligations and does not agree with the Plaintiff's claims.

Defendant Minhui Company's Defense: The tickets we sell on behalf of the principal use the code PVG to indicate the airport name. This is strictly in accordance with the regulations of the CAAC. The failure to indicate the airport name in Chinese on the ticket is not our responsibility. The Plaintiff is from Shanghai and should know that Shanghai has two airports, and tickets have a distinction between PVG and SHA. If one does not know which airport PVG and SHA represent, one can inquire by phone. The Plaintiff claims that she did not take the flight because the ticket lacked the Chinese name of the airport, but she has not provided evidence to prove the causal relationship between these two events. Therefore, we do not agree with the Plaintiff's claims.

Facts Found by the Xuhui District People's Court of Shanghai:

Defendant Minhui Company is a ticket sales agent. Plaintiff Yang Yanhui purchased from Minhui Company a 10%-discount ticket from Shanghai to Xiamen on Defendant China Southern Airlines. The ticket indicated: departure place is Shanghai PVG, departure time is 4:10 p.m. on January 30, 2003, ticket price RMB 770, non-endorsable. The ticket also contained "Air Passenger Instructions," which included provisions such as "For a refund requested within 2 hours before the scheduled departure time, a refund fee of 20% of the ticket price shall be charged." When Yang Yanhui presented this ticket at Shanghai Hongqiao Airport, airport staff informed her that she should take the flight at Shanghai Pudong Airport. Since there was no time to get to Pudong Airport, Yang Yanhui requested a transfer but was told that her ticket was a discounted ticket and could not be transferred. At 3:04 p.m., Yang Yanhui applied for a refund at the China Southern Airlines office at Hongqiao Airport and purchased a full-price ticket for a flight from Shanghai to Xiamen at 9:00 p.m. that day for RMB 850. After returning to Shanghai, Yang Yanhui demanded a full refund of the ticket price. China Southern Airlines directed her to Minhui Company for the refund, but Minhui Company stated that a refund would require a 20% service fee deducted from the ticket price, and a full refund could only be processed by the issuing airline, China Southern Airlines. Yang Yanhui, believing that the actions of China Southern Airlines and Minhui Company severely infringed upon her lawful rights and interests, initiated this lawsuit.

It was also found that the CAAC issued a "Notice on All Airlines Using Automatic Ticketing Machines to Issue Passenger Tickets in 2000" in April 2000, requiring all domestic airlines to install BSP automatic ticketing machines within 2000, and henceforth use automatic ticketing machines to issue all passenger tickets, abolishing handwritten tickets.

The above facts are confirmed by the statements of the parties, two Shanghai-to-Xiamen tickets, and the CAAC's "Notice on All Airlines Using Automatic Ticketing Machines to Issue Passenger Tickets in 2000" and other evidence.

The Xuhui District People's Court of Shanghai held that:

Article 288 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "A transport contract is a contract under which the carrier transports passengers or goods from the place of departure to the agreed destination, and the passenger, consignor, or consignee pays the fare or transportation fee." Article 293 provides: "A passenger transport contract is formed when the carrier delivers the ticket to the passenger, unless the parties have agreed otherwise or there is a different trade custom." Plaintiff Yang Yanhui, intending to travel from Shanghai to Xiamen, purchased a passenger ticket from Defendant China Southern Airlines. The passenger ticket is the evidence of the formation of the passenger transport contract. From the moment Yang Yanhui obtained the passenger ticket from China Southern Airlines, the passenger transport contract between Yang Yanhui and China Southern Airlines was formed, and Yang Yanhui and China Southern Airlines are the parties to this passenger transport contract. Defendant Minhui Company merely sold passenger tickets on behalf of China Southern Airlines based on an agency contract and is not a party to the passenger transport contract.

Contractual obligations are divided into primary obligations and collateral obligations. Primary obligations are the basic duties the debtor should perform under the contract. Collateral obligations are other duties the debtor must perform, beyond the primary obligations, to ensure the realization of the creditor's interests. Paragraph 2 of Article 60 of the Contract Law stipulates: "The parties shall abide by the principle of good faith and perform the obligations of notification, assistance, and confidentiality in accordance with the nature, purpose, and trade customs of the contract." This is the provision of the Contract Law regarding collateral obligations. In a passenger transport contract, clearly and accurately notifying passengers of transportation matters is precisely the collateral obligation that the carrier should fulfill. Only when the carrier correctly performs this collateral obligation can the passenger gather at the agreed time and place to await boarding the agreed aircraft. Shanghai has two major airports, Hongqiao and Pudong, which is indeed known to all Shanghai citizens. However, the specific codes SHA and PVG for these two airports are not universally known among Shanghai citizens. As the carrier, Defendant China Southern Airlines, based on this specific situation, should clearly indicate the airport name in the common language of China on the tickets it sells, or provide explanations in other ways sufficient for passengers to understand. By only using "Shanghai PVG" on the ticket to identify Shanghai Pudong Airport, causing Plaintiff Yang Yanhui to be unable to identify it and thus missing the agreed flight at the agreed time, China Southern Airlines should bear the fault liability for improperly performing its collateral obligation. An automatic ticketing machine is not incapable of printing Chinese characters, as evidenced by the printed Chinese characters for "Shanghai" and "Xiamen" on the ticket. Although "using automatic ticketing machines to issue all tickets" is a regulation of the CAAC, how to implement the regulations of the superior administrative authority according to local specific circumstances, so that the result of implementation better serves passengers and better fulfills the carrier's obligations under the transport contract, is the duty of China Southern Airlines as the carrier. China Southern Airlines' defense that "the ticket was issued using an automatic ticketing machine in accordance with CAAC regulations," "the automatic ticketing machine cannot print Chinese airport names on the ticket, so the airport code PVG was used," and "as the carrier, it has fulfilled its obligations" is untenable.

Article 299 of the Contract Law provides: "The carrier shall transport passengers at the time and on the flight indicated on the ticket. If the carrier delays transport, it shall, at the passenger's request, arrange for the passenger to take another flight or refund the ticket." Plaintiff Yang Yanhui held a ticket with an unclear airport name and was unable to complete the journey as scheduled. By reference to the handling method for delayed transport, Defendant China Southern Airlines should be responsible for a full refund of the ticket price and compensation for the additional expenses incurred by the passenger to reach her destination. Apart from this, Yang Yanhui's claims for compensation of other losses lack factual basis and legal grounds and are not supported.

Defendant Minhui Company is not a party to the passenger transport contract. Plaintiff Yang Yanhui's request for Minhui Company to bear civil liability for refund and compensation is not supported.

As to whether Defendants China Southern Airlines and Minhui Company must indicate the airport name in the common language of China on the tickets they sell, this should be regulated by their superior administrative authority and is not within the scope of adjudication in this case.

In conclusion, the Xuhui District People's Court of Shanghai rendered the following judgment on April 10, 2003:

1. Defendant China Southern Airlines shall, within three days from the date this judgment takes effect, refund Plaintiff Yang Yanhui the ticket price of RMB 770.
2. Defendant China Southern Airlines shall, within three days from the date this judgment takes effect, compensate Plaintiff Yang Yanhui RMB 80.
3. Plaintiff Yang Yanhui's other claims are dismissed.

Court acceptance fee of RMB 119, with Plaintiff Yang Yanhui bearing RMB 55 and Defendant China Southern Airlines bearing RMB 64.

After the first instance judgment was announced, neither party appealed, and the first instance judgment has become legally effective.

On April 28, 2003, the Xuhui District People's Court of Shanghai issued a judicial suggestion letter to the CAAC, recommending: "Where there are two or more civil airports in the same city, when airlines and passenger ticket sales agents issue tickets indicating the place of departure using airport-specific codes, they should annotate in the common language of China or provide explanations by other appropriate means, to ensure the proper performance of passenger transport contracts and enhance the good service image of China's civil aviation industry."
